title: Software Architecture Roadmap
description: A curated, stage-by-stage path from design patterns and clean code through caching, messaging, microservices, security, and system design interviews.
audience: Mid-level developers moving toward senior roles, where design decisions — not just working code — are the job.
intro: Architecture is judgement built on experience. This roadmap front-loads the principles that transfer everywhere, then applies them to increasingly realistic systems and interview scenarios.

stages.title: Patterns & Clean Code
stages.description: Start with the shared vocabulary of design and the discipline of writing code that other people can change. Everything later leans on these two.
stages.milestone: You can recognize the classic creational, structural, and behavioral patterns in real code — and explain when NOT to use one.

steps.note: Focus on recognizing patterns in the wild, not memorizing the GoF catalogue.
The senior-judgment modules are the most valuable part — read them twice.

stages.title: Caching & Messaging
stages.description: Two of the most common architectural moves: making reads fast with caches, and decoupling services with queues and event streams.
stages.milestone: You can choose between cache patterns and messaging patterns for a given problem, and state the consistency trade-offs each one accepts.

steps.note: Pay special attention to invalidation strategies — that is where caches go wrong.
Learn when a queue is enough and when an event log earns its complexity.

stages.title: Microservices & Security
stages.description: Distributed systems solve scaling problems and create new ones. Learn the microservice boundaries, communication patterns, and the security model that must wrap all of it.
stages.milestone: You can draw a service boundary for a realistic product, pick sync vs. async communication per interaction, and name the security controls each hop needs.

steps.note: The hardest stage of this roadmap — give it the time it needs.
Security questions appear in every senior interview; treat this as non-optional.

stages.title: Frontend Performance
stages.description: Architecture is not only servers. Modern senior roles expect you to reason about render performance, bundle size, and Core Web Vitals as system design.
stages.milestone: You can diagnose a slow front end with real metrics and pick fixes — code splitting, rendering strategy, caching — based on evidence.

steps.note: Even backend-leaning architects benefit — front ends are where most users feel performance.

stages.title: System Design Preparation
stages.description: Turn principles into interview performance: structured requirements, high-level design, deep dives, and the trade-off conversation interviewers are listening for.
stages.milestone: You can walk through a design in 45 minutes: clarify requirements, sketch components, pick a data model, and defend the trade-offs out loud.

steps.note: The method matters more than the examples — practice it on designs you have never seen.
Do one design per sitting, timed, before reading any solution.
Focus on the trade-off reasoning, not the specific technologies named.
Low-level design rounds test class modeling — take these after HLD feels comfortable.

stages.title: Capstone Projects
stages.description: Put everything together on realistic end-to-end projects that force architecture, implementation, and trade-off documentation at once.
stages.milestone: You have shipped a complete project you could present in a senior interview, with the decisions and compromises written down and defensible.

steps.note: Treat each phase like a real sprint — the documentation phases are the ones that matter most.
